title: The first community (Acts 2:42–47)
hook: teaching, breaking bread, prayers, and all things in common
carry: they held all things in common

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost: wind, fire, and every visitor hearing in their own language. Your line was the birthday of the church. Day seventy-four. So the Church is born. Today: what did it actually look like on an ordinary Tuesday?

Anyone have a ladder? A cup of sugar? A ride to the airport on Thursday? The group chat for a building or a street runs on questions like that, and usually somebody answers. Now take it all the way. Luke says that after Pentecost about three thousand people were baptized in a single day. A small group from Galilee became a crowd. So what did they do next? Luke answers in one short paragraph, six verses long. Today: the first community.
screen: `ANYONE HAVE A LADDER?` → `THREE THOUSAND IN A DAY.` → `SIX VERSES FROM LUKE.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of it, in the Douay-Rheims: "And they were persevering in the doctrine of the apostles, and in the communication of the breaking of bread, and in prayers." In Luke's Greek, that's four things. The apostles' teaching: they kept learning. Fellowship, which is the Greek word koinonia, sharing, having a part in each other. The breaking of bread: meals together, and, as Catholics read it, the Eucharist. And the prayers, including, Luke says, going up to the temple every day. They were Jews, and they kept praying where they always had. Then this: "And all they that believed, were together, and had all things common." They sold property and possessions and handed out the money to anyone in need. Luke says they ate with glad and simple hearts, and people liked them. Now, the honest reading. This wasn't a system anyone was forced into. A few chapters later Peter tells a man that his land was his own to keep. Giving was free. Not every church since has lived exactly like this. Catholic religious life draws on it: monks and nuns vow to hold their goods in common. And the Church teaches something for everyone: that the goods of the earth are meant, in the end, for all people, so what you own is also held for others. Four pillars, and one open hand.
screen: `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYERS.` · `KOINONIA: HAVING A PART IN EACH OTHER.` · `ALL THINGS COMMON, FREELY GIVEN.` · `MONKS, NUNS, AND EVERYONE ELSE.` · then, large: `AND HAD ALL THINGS COMMON.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: find one thing you could share. Settle and breathe. Walk through your home in your mind, room by room. Somewhere there's a thing you own that sits unused while someone else could use it: a coat, a tool, a book, a spare hour on Saturday. Don't pick the thing that's easiest to get rid of. Pick the thing that would actually help someone. Hold it in your mind. If you pray, you can ask who it's meant for. The bell holds the time.
koinonia. The Greek word for fellowship, for sharing a part in each other's lives, one mark of the first believers.
Your line: they held all things in common. Today, lend or give away the one thing you found, to someone who can use it. Day seventy-four.

howItsDone: Catholic religious communities hold their goods in common, and parishes gather around the same four things: teaching, fellowship, the Eucharist and prayer, with collections and ministries for people in need.

fork.setup: you're one of the three thousand, newly baptized. you own a field, and people in the community are going hungry. what does Luke say people did?

fork.reveal: they sold possessions and handed the money out as anyone had need, freely. and they ate together with glad and simple hearts.

original.note: Greek: fellowship, sharing, having a part in something together. one of the four marks of the first community.

trapdoor: what you thought: the first Christians were a commune.
what it means: a community built on four things, teaching, fellowship, bread and prayer, where people freely gave so no one went without.
what a scholar hears: koinonia, a word for partnership and shared goods. and Catholic teaching draws from it the universal destination of goods: what you own is also for others.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of Acts 2:42 and 2:44 given from memory; confirm.
The Douay-Rheims 2:42 'communication of the breaking of bread' joins fellowship and the breaking of bread; the script counts four things following the Greek. Confirm the explanation is fair.
Acts 5:4 (Ananias's property was his own) used to show the giving was voluntary; confirm.
Universal destination of goods: CCC 2402–2404. Confirm.
'The breaking of bread: meals together, and the Eucharist' — Catholic reading; confirm.
